abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for geometric visual representation learning that fundamentally reconceptualizes how deep neural networks encode spatial structure in images. Unlike conventional data-driven approaches that treat geometry as an emergent property, we propose an explicit geometric prior injection mechanism based on Lie group theory. Our framework establishes a mathematical isomorphism between the image transformation group and the representation embedding space, providing rigorous theoretical guarantees for geometric invariance and equivariance. The key contribution lies in deriving a unified geometric consistency loss that simultaneously enforces transformation covariance at multiple scales, enabling the network to learn hierarchically structured visual features with explicit geometric meaning. We prove theoretically that this approach converges to a geometrically consistent minimum and provides bounds on generalization error. Extensive experiments on 3D vision tasks including depth estimation, pose estimation, and scene reconstruction demonstrate that our paradigm achieves substantial improvements over existing methods, with a 12.8% reduction in geometric error on KITTI and 8.4% improvement in accuracy on Pascal3D+. This work introduces a paradigm shift from purely data-driven to geometry-informed vision representation, opening new research directions for structured visual understanding.

Despite the empirical success of self-supervised learning in computer vision, existing contrastive frameworks lack rigorous theoretical analysis of why geometric transformations improve representation quality. This paper provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of geometric invariance in self-supervised visual representation learning and derives principled guidelines for transformation selection. We formulate the learning objective as a contrastive estimation problem in the space of geometric orbits and prove that geometric invariance emerges naturally when transformationaugmented views preserve the semantic structure of the representation manifold. Our analysis reveals that the effectiveness of geometric augmentations depends critically on the spectral properties of the underlying data graph, leading to a novel adaptive augmentation strategy that dynamically selects transformations based on estimated manifold curvature. We further derive convergence bounds for the proposed method and show that adaptive geometric augmentation achieves tighter representation bounds compared to fixed augmentation policies. Experiments on ImageNet, COCO, and downstream visual reasoning tasks demonstrate that our theoretically-grounded approach achieves 3.2% improvement in linear probe accuracy over MoCo v3 and 5.7% improvement in transfer learning performance, validating our theoretical predictions.

We present Hierarchical Event Understanding Surveillance System (HEUSS), a novel paradigm for intelligent visual surveillance that moves beyond traditional pipeline-based tracking and recognition approaches. HEUSS introduces a unified cognitive architecture that integrates spatial scene understanding, temporal motion analysis, and semantic event recognition within a single differentiable framework. The system employs a hierarchical graph neural network that models surveillance scenes at three distinct levels: low-level spatial graphs capturing object relationships, mid-level temporal graphs encoding motion trajectories, and high-level semantic hypergraphs representing complex event patterns. A key architectural innovation is the cross-level attention mechanism that enables bidirectional information flow between spatial entities and semantic concepts, allowing the system to reason about complex multi-agent interactions and context-dependent behaviors. The framework incorporates a learned knowledge base of typical surveillance scenarios that guides bottom-up perception and top-down inference. Extensive evaluation on CDNET, Avenue, and Shanghai Tech benchmarks demonstrates that HEUSS achieves state-of-the-art performance in anomaly detection, with 8.7% improvement in frame-level accuracy and 12.3% improvement in pixel-level precision. This work establishes a new paradigm for integrated visual surveillance with cognitive reasoning capabilities.

Multi-object tracking in dense scenes remains challenging due to frequent occlusions, ambiguous appearances, and complex motion patterns. This paper presents Unified Appearance-Motion Tracking System (UAMTS), a novel tracking framework that significantly advances state-of-the-art performance through innovative integration of appearance modeling and motion prediction. UAMTS introduces a dual-stream architecture consisting of a geometric-aware appearance encoder that captures discriminative object features invariant to viewpoint and illumination changes, and a physics-informed motion predictor that models object dynamics using learned differential equations. The system employs a novel temporal association module that resolves occlusions by reasoning about both visual similarity and physical plausibility of predicted trajectories. An adaptive track management scheme dynamically adjusts tracking parameters based on scene density and occlusion statistics. We also introduce a hard example mining strategy that focuses training on difficult occlusion cases. Comprehensive experiments on MOT17, MOT20, and DanceTrack demonstrate substantial improvements. UAMTS achieves 3.2% relative improvement in MOTA over ByteTrack on MOT17, with particularly notable gains in scenarios involving prolonged occlusions where ID switch reduction exceeds 35%. Ablation studies confirm the complementary nature of appearance and motion streams.
